items.definition: Short-range, low-power wireless for connecting devices directly, usually up to about 10 m.
items.examples: Wireless earbuds; a Bluetooth keyboard; a smartwatch.
items.examTip: Short range, low power, pairing. Slower than Wi-Fi.
keyFacts: Range about 10 m (up to 100 m on newer versions), so it suits devices kept close to the user
Low power, so it suits wearables and peripherals that run on small batteries
Devices must pair first, so random devices can't connect without the user agreeing
Risks include bluejacking (unwanted messages) and bluesnarfing (data theft), so turn it off when not in use

items.definition: A wired standard that transfers data and power between a device and a computer.
items.examples: A flash drive; charging a phone over USB-C; a printer.
items.examTip: Wired, direct, fast, no network needed. Newer versions are much faster.
keyFacts: USB 2.0 runs at 480 Mbps and USB 3.x at 5–10 Gbps, so newer ports move large files much faster
Also charges devices, so one cable carries both power and data
Plug and play, so devices work as soon as they're connected without manual set-up
Infected sticks can bring in malware, which is why some organisations block USB ports

items.definition: Wireless networking by radio, connecting devices to a router or access point.
items.examples: Office or school Wi-Fi; a café hotspot.
items.examTip: Mobility vs Ethernet's speed, reliability and security. Public Wi-Fi is a risk.
keyFacts: Range about 30–50 m indoors, reduced by walls, so large buildings need several access points
2.4 GHz reaches further but is slower; 5 GHz is faster but shorter range, so the choice depends on the room
Use WPA3, because WEP is insecure and can be cracked in minutes
Speed is shared between all devices, so the network slows down as more people connect

items.definition: Wired networking using copper or fibre-optic cables.
items.examples: Office PCs cabled to a switch; fibre between buildings.
items.examTip: For fixed devices it is faster, more reliable and more secure than Wi-Fi.
keyFacts: Typically 1 Gbps, and fibre is much faster over long distances, so it suits busy networks and servers
Low latency, so it is good for video calls and gaming where delay is noticeable
Hard to intercept and free of radio interference, so it is more secure and reliable than wireless
Needs cabling, so it is less flexible: devices are tied to where the sockets are

comparisonTable.title: Connection Methods Compared: Bluetooth vs USB vs Wi-Fi vs Ethernet
rows: Lower — signal can be intercepted; WPA3 helps

subtopics.title: How Connection Types Meet User/Organisation Needs

items.term: Matching Connection Types to User and Organisation Needs
items.definition: The right connection depends on the need: speed, mobility, range, cost, security and number of devices.
items.examples: Ethernet for hospital equipment; Wi-Fi in a café; Bluetooth handheld scanners.
items.examTip: Justify the choice by linking a technical feature to the scenario's need.
keyFacts: Mobile workers need Wi-Fi, so they can move around the building and stay connected
Fixed, reliable workstations suit Ethernet, because a cable gives steady speed with no interference
Short-range peripherals suit Bluetooth, because it is low power and needs no cables
Servers and the backbone suit fibre, because they carry the most traffic and need the highest speed

subtopics.title: Implications of Selecting Different Connection Types

items.term: Implications of Selecting and Using Different Connection Types
items.definition: Choosing a connection affects security, cost, maintenance and flexibility, not just speed.
items.examples: All-Wi-Fi saves cabling but adds risk; blocking USB stops theft but complicates printing.
items.examTip: For "implications" questions cover security, cost, performance and users.
keyFacts: Wi-Fi is easy to install but less secure, because signals reach beyond the building and can be picked up
Ethernet needs costly cabling but is reliable, so it costs more up front but gives fewer problems
USB may need blocking to stop malware, which can inconvenience staff who rely on memory sticks
Wireless depends on signal quality, so walls and distance can cause slow or dropped connections

subtopics.title: Impact of Connection Types on IT System Performance

items.term: How Connection Types Affect IT System Performance
items.definition: The connection type affects the speed, latency, reliability and capacity of a system.
items.examples: Switching video editors from Wi-Fi to Ethernet cuts transfer times.
items.examTip: Link a metric to the connection: Ethernet low latency; Wi-Fi varies; Bluetooth low bandwidth.
keyFacts: Wired has lower latency, because there is no radio signal to process or retransmit
Wired is more reliable because there is no interference, so connections don't drop
Wi-Fi bandwidth is shared between users, so each person gets less speed as more people connect
Jitter on Wi-Fi hurts calls, because uneven delay makes voices break up

items.definition: Every device has its own cable to a central switch.
items.examples: An office where each PC and printer connects to one switch.
items.examTip: One cable fails → one device down. Central switch fails → everything down.
keyFacts: Most common topology, because it is reliable and easy to manage
Easy to add devices and find faults, because each device has its own cable to the switch
The switch is a single point of failure: if it fails, every device loses the network
Uses more cable than bus, so it costs more to install

items.definition: Devices connected in a closed loop; data travels around it in one direction.
items.examples: Old token ring networks.
items.examTip: One break can stop the whole ring. Largely obsolete.
keyFacts: Each device links to two neighbours, so data passes through every device on the way round
Token passing prevents collisions, because only the device holding the token can send
Adding devices disrupts the ring, because the loop must be broken to connect them
A dual ring adds backup, so data can go the other way if one cable breaks

items.definition: All devices share one backbone cable; every device receives the data.
items.examples: Early coaxial Ethernet networks.
items.examTip: Cheap, but a cable break takes down the whole network.
keyFacts: Cheap because it needs minimal cabling, so it suits small, temporary networks
Only one device can transmit at a time, otherwise signals collide on the shared cable
Slows down as devices are added, because more devices compete for the same cable
Needs terminators at each end, so signals don't bounce back and corrupt data

comparisonTable.title: Network Topologies Compared
rows: All devices connect to central switch
All devices on one shared backbone cable
Degrades — collisions increase with more devices
Higher cabling cost (individual cables to centre)

items.definition: A tiny network of one person's devices, usually by Bluetooth, within about 10 m.
items.examples: A phone linked to earbuds and a smartwatch.
items.examTip: The smallest network: just your own devices.
keyFacts: Range about 10 m, so it only links devices one person carries or uses nearby
Mainly Bluetooth or USB, connecting things like phones, earbuds and smartwatches
No infrastructure needed, so there are no switches or routers to buy

items.definition: A network covering one site, such as a building, with hardware the organisation owns.
items.examples: A school network; an office network.
items.examTip: One site, owned hardware, fast.
keyFacts: The organisation owns the switches, cables and access points, so it controls security and set-up
Fast (about 1 Gbps wired) with low latency, so files and apps on the network open quickly
Wired and/or wireless, so it can mix fixed desktops with mobile devices
Connects to the internet through a router, which links the private LAN to the outside world

items.definition: A network over a large area that links LANs using leased third-party lines.
items.examples: A bank linking all its branches; the internet.
items.examTip: Unlike a LAN, the organisation does not own the infrastructure.
keyFacts: Covers cities, countries or continents, so an organisation's sites can share systems and data
Uses leased lines from telecoms providers, because organisations can't lay cables that far themselves
Slower and higher latency than a LAN, because data travels long distances through many devices
Ongoing rental costs, because the lines are leased, not owned

items.definition: An encrypted tunnel through the internet that connects users securely to a private network.
items.examples: Remote staff on the intranet; linking offices without leased lines.
items.examTip: Not a physical network: it runs over the internet, so it is cheaper than a leased WAN.
keyFacts: Data inside the tunnel is encrypted, so it can't be read if intercepted on the internet
Users must authenticate, so only authorised people can reach the private network
Cheaper than leased WAN lines, because it uses the ordinary internet connection
Encryption adds some delay, because every packet must be encrypted and decrypted

comparisonTable.title: Network Types Compared: PAN vs LAN vs WAN vs VPN
rows: Secure remote access / site-to-site over internet

items.definition: What users need: mobility, the applications they run, and how many connect at once.
items.examTip: The starting point for any network choice: what do users actually need to do?
keyFacts: More users need more bandwidth, otherwise everyone's connection slows down
Mobile users need wireless, so they can work from anywhere in the building
Real-time apps need low latency, so video calls and VoIP don't lag
Remote access needs a VPN, so staff outside the office connect securely

items.definition: Technical requirements the network must meet, e.g. speed, latency and uptime.
items.examTip: Turn user needs into numbers: bandwidth, latency, uptime.
keyFacts: Minimum bandwidth for all users, so the network stays usable at its busiest
Low latency for real-time apps, so calls and live systems respond without delay
Uptime targets (e.g. 99.99%), so critical services are almost never unavailable
Room to grow in 3–5 years, so the network doesn't need replacing as the organisation expands

items.definition: Whether every device and site that needs to connect can do so reliably.
items.examTip: Can everything that needs to connect, connect?
keyFacts: Must support PCs, phones, printers and IoT, so every device staff rely on can connect
Multiple sites need a WAN or VPN, so branches can share systems and data
4G/5G as backup if broadband fails, so the organisation can keep working during an outage

items.definition: The full cost of building and running a network: hardware, cabling, fees and support.
items.examTip: Split into one-off capital costs and ongoing running costs.
keyFacts: One-off costs: switches, routers and cabling, paid up front when the network is built
Ongoing costs: ISP fees, leased lines and support, paid for as long as the network runs
VPN is cheaper than leased lines, because it uses the existing internet connection
Wireless saves cabling, so it is cheaper to install, especially in older buildings

items.definition: How well the network uses its bandwidth to avoid congestion and delays.
items.examTip: QoS prioritises important traffic such as calls.
keyFacts: QoS puts calls and video first, so they stay smooth even when the network is busy
Segmenting the network reduces congestion, because traffic stays within its own section
Monitoring finds bottlenecks, so problems are fixed before users notice them

items.definition: Whether the network works with the hardware, software and protocols already in use.
items.examTip: An incompatible network is useless however fast it is.
keyFacts: Older systems may need old protocols, so a new network must still support them or they stop working
New switches must suit existing devices, otherwise hardware already owned may need replacing
Management tools must work on all systems, so IT staff can monitor everything from one place

items.definition: Practicalities of rollout: how long it takes, how it is tested and how much disruption it causes.
items.examTip: Cover all three: timescales, testing and downtime.
keyFacts: Large installs take weeks or months, so they must be planned around the organisation's busy times
Test before switching over, so faults are found before staff depend on the new network
Reduce downtime with out-of-hours or phased rollout, so work carries on during the change
Have a fallback plan, so the old network can be restored if the new one fails

items.definition: How the network affects how much staff can get done.
items.examTip: Link slow networks to real costs: missed deadlines, complaints, lost revenue.
keyFacts: A fast, reliable network boosts output, because staff aren't waiting for files or systems
Downtime wastes paid time, because staff are paid but can't do their work
Remote work depends on VPN and internet quality, so a poor connection makes home workers less productive

items.definition: Protecting the network from unauthorised access, interception and attack.
items.examTip: Wireless is more vulnerable than wired. Key needs: WPA3, firewall, VPN.
keyFacts: Use WPA3 on Wi-Fi, because WEP is obsolete and easily cracked
Separate guest Wi-Fi from the staff network, so visitors can't reach internal systems
Firewall at the edge, so traffic from the internet is filtered before it reaches the network
VPN for remote access, so staff working away from the office connect securely

items.term: How Features of a Network and Component Parts Affect Performance
items.definition: Network speed, latency and reliability depend on hardware, topology, connection type and set-up.
items.examples: Upgrading a 100 Mbps switch to 1 Gbps; adding access points to ease Wi-Fi congestion.
items.examTip: Cover speed, latency, reliability and how the number of users affects them.
keyFacts: Faster switches increase throughput, so more data moves across the network at once
Cable type matters: fibre > Cat6 > Cat5e, so better cable gives higher speeds over longer runs
More users means less bandwidth each, so a network that is fine for 10 may struggle with 100
Access point placement affects Wi-Fi coverage, so badly placed APs leave dead spots

topics.title: Issues Relating to Transmission of Data

items.definition: SMTP sends email; POP3 and IMAP retrieve it from the mail server.
items.examples: Outlook sending with SMTP; a phone syncing with IMAP.
items.examTip: IMAP keeps mail on the server (syncs all devices); POP3 downloads it to one device.
keyFacts: SMTP sends email from the sender's device to the mail server and on to the recipient's server
POP3 downloads to one device and usually deletes from the server, so mail isn't available elsewhere
IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it, so the same inbox shows on every device

comparisonTable.title: Email Protocols Compared: SMTP vs POP3 vs IMAP
rows: Downloaded to local device; deleted from server (by default)
Kept on mail server; synced to devices
No — email on one device only
Yes — same inbox on all devices
Yes — all mail stays on server
Single-device users with limited server storage
Multi-device users wanting consistent inbox everywhere
Sending from Outlook to Gmail server

items.term: Voice and Video Calls over the Internet (VoIP)
items.definition: Voice and video calls sent as data packets over the internet instead of phone lines.
items.examples: Teams, Zoom and WhatsApp calls.
items.examTip: Needs enough bandwidth AND low latency, or calls lag and break up.
keyFacts: Much cheaper than phone calls, especially abroad, because calls travel as ordinary internet data
High latency causes delays, so people talk over each other
Packet loss causes dropouts, so words or video frames go missing
QoS prioritises voice traffic, so calls stay clear even when the network is busy

items.definition: HTTP is how browsers request web pages; HTTPS adds TLS encryption.
items.examples: A news site over HTTP; online banking over HTTPS.
items.examTip: HTTPS adds encryption, integrity and authentication.
keyFacts: HTTP uses port 80 and HTTPS uses port 443, so firewalls can tell the two kinds of traffic apart
HTTPS needs a digital certificate, which proves the site is genuine and enables encryption
Browsers mark HTTP sites 'Not Secure', which warns users not to enter personal details

comparisonTable.title: HTTP vs HTTPS
rows: TLS/SSL encrypts all data in transit
No — data can be modified in transit
Credentials and data visible to anyone intercepting traffic
Public content with no login (increasingly replaced by HTTPS)
Any page with login, personal data, or payment
E-commerce, banking, login pages, all modern sites

items.definition: Technology that protects online card payments, e.g. encryption and tokenisation.
items.examples: Apple Pay tokens; 3D Secure codes at checkout.
items.examTip: Layers: HTTPS, tokenisation, extra authentication and PCI DSS rules.
keyFacts: HTTPS encrypts card details in transit, so they can't be read if intercepted
Tokenisation means the merchant never sees the real card number, so a breach can't leak it
PCI DSS sets rules for handling card data, so businesses that take cards must follow them
3D Secure adds an extra check (e.g. a code from the bank), so a stolen card number alone isn't enough

items.definition: Data in transit can be intercepted, altered or blocked, especially if unencrypted.
items.examples: Sniffing logins on open public Wi-Fi.
items.examTip: The fix for most transmission risks is encryption: TLS, HTTPS or a VPN.
keyFacts: Packet sniffing reads unencrypted data, so passwords sent in plain text can be captured
Man-in-the-middle intercepts and relays traffic, so the attacker can read or change it unnoticed
Evil twin is a fake Wi-Fi hotspot, so users who connect send all their traffic through the attacker
Fix with HTTPS and a VPN on public Wi-Fi, so intercepted data is encrypted and useless

items.term: Factors Affecting and Implications of Bandwidth and Latency
items.definition: Bandwidth is how much data can be sent per second; latency is the delay before it arrives.
items.examples: Fast broadband that still lags in games; school Wi-Fi slowing at lunch.
items.examTip: They are different. High bandwidth doesn't help if latency is high. Explain the effect on users.
keyFacts: Bandwidth is shared between users, so each person's speed drops as more people use the network
Latency comes from distance, hops and congestion, so far-away servers respond more slowly
Low latency matters for calls and gaming, because delay makes them hard to use
Jitter is varying latency, which makes calls choppy because packets arrive unevenly

subtopics.title: File Types and Formats for Transmission

items.definition: Image formats differ in file size, quality and features such as transparency.
items.examples: JPEG photos; PNG logos; GIF animations.
items.examTip: Choose for the scenario: JPEG for photos, PNG for transparency, SVG for scalable logos.
keyFacts: JPEG is lossy and small, so it suits photos on websites where fast loading matters
PNG is lossless with transparency, so it suits logos and graphics that need sharp edges
GIF has only 256 colours but supports simple animation, so it suits small animated images
RAW is huge but keeps maximum quality, so photographers use it for editing

items.definition: Audio formats differ in quality and size depending on compression.
items.examples: MP3 streaming; WAV in a recording studio.
items.examTip: MP3 = small, for streaming. WAV/FLAC = full quality, for production.
keyFacts: MP3 is lossy, small and widely supported, so it plays on almost any device
AAC is lossy but sounds better than MP3 at the same size, so streaming services use it
WAV is uncompressed and large, so it suits editing where full quality is needed
FLAC is lossless but smaller than WAV, so it suits storing music at full quality

items.definition: A video file is a container (e.g. MP4) holding streams compressed by a codec.
items.examples: MP4 on YouTube; MOV from an iPhone.
items.examTip: Container holds the streams; the codec compresses them.
keyFacts: MP4 is the most compatible, so it plays on almost every device and website
MKV holds multiple audio and subtitle tracks, so it suits films in several languages
MOV is Apple's high-quality format, so it suits editing on Apple devices
Higher bitrate gives better quality but needs more bandwidth and storage

items.definition: Installer and program files specific to each operating system.
items.examples: .exe on Windows; .apk on Android; .dmg on macOS.
items.examTip: Large downloads; malware is often disguised as software.
keyFacts: EXE/MSI are Windows installers, so they won't run on other operating systems
APK installs Android apps, usually from the Play Store
DMG is used for macOS apps, so Mac users can install software
Check the source and digital signature before running, because installers can contain malware

comparisonTable.title: File Formats Summary by Media Type
rows: JPEG smallest for web photos; PNG needed for logos/transparency
MP3 for streaming; WAV/FLAC for production — much larger
None commonly — all video is compressed
H.265 half the size of H.264; bitrate controls quality vs bandwidth
EXE, APK, DMG, DEB (+ ZIP wrappers)
Large files need reliable connection; verify digital signature

items.definition: Makes files smaller by permanently removing some data.
items.examples: JPEG photos; MP3 music; streamed video.
items.examTip: Smaller but lower quality, and irreversible. Never for text, code or medical images.
keyFacts: The original cannot be rebuilt, because the removed data is gone for good
Much smaller files than lossless, so they download and stream quickly
Quality drops each re-save, because more data is removed every time
Used for web images and streaming, where small size matters more than perfect quality

items.definition: Makes files smaller without losing any data; the original is restored exactly.
items.examples: ZIP archives; PNG images; FLAC audio.
items.examTip: Needed wherever accuracy matters: text, code, spreadsheets, medical images.
keyFacts: Original restored perfectly, so it suits text, code and data where every bit matters
Less compression than lossy, so files stay larger
Works on any file type, e.g. ZIP files, because nothing is thrown away

comparisonTable.title: Lossy vs Lossless Compression
rows: Moderate — smaller but not as dramatically
Reduced — degradation increases with compression level
None — identical to original after decompression
Text, code, executables, archives, where accuracy matters
Medical images, legal documents, scientific data, text
Cases where file size is critical and quality loss acceptable
PNG, FLAC, WAV, ZIP, RAR, GIF (images)

items.definition: Software that compresses audio/video for sending and decompresses it for playback.
items.examples: H.264 for video; MP3 and AAC for audio.
items.examTip: Codec = coder + decoder. Without the right codec, a file won't play.
keyFacts: The encoder compresses and the decoder decompresses, so video can be sent and then played back
Sender and receiver need the same codec, otherwise the file won't play
More compression needs more processing, so older devices may struggle to play newer codecs
H.265 files are about half the size of H.264 at the same quality, so they save bandwidth and storage
